page: UpCloud CLOUDNATIVE-8xCPU-16GB is a Cloud Native family virtual server built on the KVM hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an AMD EPYC 7542 processor running at 2.0 GHz. The configuration includes 8 shared vCPUs (8 physical cores with 1.0 thread per core) and 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding 2.0 GB of RAM per core. Cache specifications consist of 64 KB L1d, 0.5 MB L2, and 16 MB L3 cache. The hardware supports AVX, AES, SHA_NI, BMI2, ADX, and FMA instruction sets, but lacks AVX-512 and AMX capabilities. No local storage or GPU hardware is bundled with this instance, though it includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark data reveals distinct performance tradeoffs, particularly regarding the shared CPU allocation. In raw compute tests, the server exhibits poor single-core performance with a stress-ng score of 781.19 (bottom 10%) and a weak multi-core score of 6000.74 (bottom 25%). Memory performance is mixed; while small-block read-only memory bandwidth is average at 825.47 GB/sec, large-block uncached read and write bandwidths fall into the bottom 25% at 30.23 GB/sec and 17.66 GB/sec respectively. Despite these constraints, the server achieves average tier results in Geekbench multi-core (6083.0), software compilation (9302.0), and Redis SET operations (11.14 million operations per second). Large-model LLM inference is highly constrained, with the 7B model managing only 7.89 tokens per second for text generation.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the shared CPU model and lack of local storage position this server as a budget-oriented option for resource-dense, non-continuous workloads. The 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio provides a high core count relative to memory, making it suitable for multi-threaded tasks that are not execution-time critical. Appropriate workloads include software compilation, text processing, basic database operations, and lightweight web serving, whereas intensive real-time compute, large-scale LLM deployment, and high-throughput storage tasks are limited by the shared resource model and weak uncached memory bandwidth.
